Abstract
Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), LINE-1 elements, and other endogenously active transposable-element families are now being studied for their role as a potential interface between epigenetic control and innate immunity. Here, we discuss how locus-specific failures in repressive complexes containing ATRX–DAXX–H3.3 and TRIM28–SETDB1–H3K9me3 may allow these elements to enter into unique molecular states that include double-stranded RNA, DNA/RNA hybrid molecules, RNA–protein complexes, reverse-transcription products, and RNA. Each of these states differs from the others in terms of its persistence, structural characteristics, and accessibility to sensors such as MDA5, RIG-I, cGAS–STING, and ZBP1, as well as host restriction pathways. We also emphasize that simply expressing a retroelement does not imply that it is competent to bind to a sensor and/or undergo productive retrotransposition. Rather, a distinction needs to be made between intermediate stages in the process of retrotransposition and productive retrotransposition itself. Therefore, the evidence needed to assign a specific sensor to a particular retroelement product must be presented. Furthermore, persistent stress caused by retroelement activity could converge with multiple cellular processes, such as p53–CDKN1A/p21-mediated cell-cycle arrest, PML-mediated nuclear organization, and lysosomal or metabolism-based changes leading to long-lived microglial states; however, demonstrating path dependence after removing the initiating perturbation would be required to demonstrate true hysteresis. In addition, HP1 proteins extend the repressive environment by interacting with H3K9me3 through their chromodomains and converting what would otherwise be a covalently modified histone into a multivalent protein complex. Upon interaction with H3K9me3, HP1γ utilizes its chromoshadow domain to interact with SUV420H2 [
68
]. Interaction with HP1γ enables deposition of H4K20me3 through hydrophobic surface contacts involving HP1γ residues I165, F167, and L172. Therefore, heterochromatin formation may depend on specific residue-level protein–protein interactions rather than generalized chromatin compaction alone. HP1β is also involved in maintaining DNA methylation [
69
].
Therefore, the interdependencies among these architectural components can be represented schematically as follows:
SETDB1 → H3K9me3 → HP1 association → SUV420H2 recruitment → deposition of H4K20me3
Furthermore, HP1 facilitates maintenance of CpG methylation as well as supporting other types of repressive marks and higher-order chromatin organization [
70
].
As previously mentioned, the relationships described above create local epigenetic cooperation. The presence of H3K9me3 at a particular genomic location creates opportunities for HP1 association at that location. Association of HP1 with a particular location can facilitate higher-order chromatin organization as well as promotion of other types of repressive marks [

8. Conclusions—The Genome–Immunity Boundary
Increasingly, the “repetitive genome” is being understood as a physically regulated compartment with important implications for both neuroimmune function in the brain and immune homeostasis outside the brain. In addition to a number of other molecular checkpoints, many of which act sequentially, there are several checkpoints that control the physical compartmentalization of this genome. Specifically, these checkpoints include repression of chromatin, RNA processing, structural regulation of processed RNAs, regulation of RNP formation, restriction of reverse transcription, degradation of aberrant intermediate nucleic-acid structures, and termination of the cellular state established as a result of the generation of those structures. As a consequence, pathology may occur when one or more of these checkpoints fail to prevent endogenous sequences from acquiring physical molecular characteristics that are recognizable as foreign by the host’s surveillance systems.
It is therefore essential that we redirect our focus of study away from repeat families toward specific molecular states that are established independently by each locus. Unexpressed ERVs, autonomously transcribed ERVs, ERV-derived double-stranded RNA molecules, RNA–DNA hybrids, LINE-1 RNA molecules, ORF1p-containing RNPs, ORF2p activity, recently synthesized cDNA, and fully integrated new genomic elements are examples of discrete biochemical states with unique lifespans, subcellular locations, and capacities to contribute to pathological processes.
